Kujo vs Bend: workflow evidence and language proofs
Compare Kujo’s language and workflow tools with current Bend’s laws, proofs and parallel execution, including scope and limitations.

Kujo and Bend check agent-written software at different levels. Bend lets you state laws and check proofs in the language. Kujo combines language checks with separate tools for task requirements, output checks and execution records. Choose based on what you need to verify, and consider using both when the requirement spans these levels.

Bend’s guide describes a pure, affine, dependently typed language with explicit IO. It documents native CPU and GPU execution, while its JavaScript target runs parallel calls sequentially. Bend pairs laws with proof definitions; the negative fixture we inspected rejects an unfinished claim used as a proof. Kujo provides runtime execution and type diagnostics, but a successful `kujo check` does not establish type correctness in 1.8.2. Spec, Eval and Workcell are separate tools that check other parts of the workflow.

Evaluate Kujo when you need to define an automation task, check its files or command results and keep evidence of the run. Start with one acceptance criterion and an incorrect output that the checker must reject. Allow time to choose, configure and pin the separate tools: installing Kujo does not automatically set up a release gate.

Evaluate Bend when you can state the central requirement precisely and prove it within the supported language subset. Its guide emphasizes proof construction and balanced parallel computation. This can suit mathematical invariants, but you will need to learn its affine programming model, write explicit annotations and maintain the proofs.

You could place a Bend component behind a process or file interface and check the surrounding workflow with other tools. We did not test a Kujo–Bend adapter. Keep proof results separate from integration tests: a proof about the component does not show that the application calls it correctly.

Bend excludes unsafe and foreign code from its stronger proof verdict. Its guide also says that translation into the small kernel is not itself proven. Kujo’s output checks cover the assertions and runs you define, rather than every possible input. In either case, review whether the specification expresses the requirement fully.

Bend 2.0.37 accepted a valid proof through --verdict with its independent BendTT kernel built using Lean 4.34.0. Calling that kernel directly accepted the exported proof and rejected a corrupted proof body. Broken proof, type and affine-use fixtures also failed. A fork-join example returned 4096 through native CPU and sequential JavaScript targets. These tests check results, not parallel speedup, GPU execution or the unproven translation into the kernel.
Stable v2.0.37 (2026-10-13; release commit 4ff8545f19b09b7d2b8ca2303668100eac8efd66). Release binaries tested on macOS and Linux x86_64; independent kernel built with Lean 4.34.0.
Laws and proof checking for agent-authored programs, with parallel execution.
Type-level laws paired with proof definitions; open claims are rejected when used as proof.
The independent BendTT kernel accepted a valid exported proof and rejected a corrupted proof body. Its guarantee still depends on the documented trust boundaries.
Native CPU and sequential JavaScript results tested, including fork-join syntax. GPU support is documented but was not executed; no speedup was measured.
A Kujo-style cross-tool receipt system was not verified. Proof-checker output has a different scope.
Is Bend only the older HVM language?

This comparison uses the project linked by bend-lang.org today: bendlang/bend and its current laws-and-proofs guide. Older HVM-era descriptions do not establish the capabilities of this reviewed version.
Does Kujo offer the same proof guarantee?
This review did not establish an equivalent general proof system in Kujo. Kujo’s task and outcome checks should be judged by the concrete conditions they validate.
Compare what Bend can prove with what Kujo’s workflow checks can verify.
Is the requirement a mathematical property, an observed outcome, or both?
Bend makes effects and value reuse explicit

Bend separates pure computation from explicit IO. Affine values constrain reuse; copyable data and annotations affect how functions are written. A team coming from ordinary imperative code should trial the data model before estimating migration effort.
A proof-friendly component still needs an IO boundary and tests for its callers.
Review what the law actually promises

Bend checks proof definitions against type-level laws. The inspected negative fixture rejects an open claim offered as a proof. Unsafe and foreign code sit outside the stronger guarantee, and the guide identifies an unproven translation into the small kernel.
Review the law and trusted boundary as carefully as the generated implementation.
Match the workload to the parallel target

The guide documents CPU and GPU execution, with sequential JavaScript output. Parallel calls suit independent, balanced work; target choice and workload shape belong in the evaluation. No relative speed measurement was performed here.
Keep correctness evidence separate from target-specific latency and throughput measurements.
Use workflow checks to verify integration artifacts and retain the run.
Evaluate a precisely stated law and its checked proof.

Write a component law and a separate integration acceptance criterion. Explain which inputs the law quantifies over and which external effects remain outside it.

Use the pinned guide and negative fixture as starting evidence. Our 2.0.37 trial rejected a broken proof and an unfilled law. Reproduce both on your own toolchain, and distinguish --check-only from the separate --verdict kernel step.
Feed a known wrong artifact to an independent check. Exercise the caller and serialization path so that a valid component cannot hide a broken integration.
Record the proof result, integration result and performance measurement separately. Accept only the guarantee each check actually establishes.
Kujo vs BAML: comparing agent development workflows
Compare current BAML and Kujo across type checking, evaluations, execution evidence, adoption and the boundaries of each toolchain.

Current BAML is a language for agents, with its own runtime and bridges into other languages. Kujo is also a programming language, with separate tools for defining tasks, checking outputs and recording runs. Compare them on the same application requirement, including the work needed to integrate and maintain each option.

The BAML source we reviewed contains a compiler, a check command that collects project diagnostics and a test command that runs compiled test sets. Its current website describes typed AI functions, concurrency and tracing. These claims do not establish a speed advantage over Kujo. Kujo handles language execution in its runtime and provides task contracts and run records through separately versioned tools.

Consider Kujo when you need explicit acceptance criteria, checks of files and processes, and run evidence you can inspect without a hosted dashboard. Include the cost of configuring and maintaining those tools. A ledger entry marked pass should link to the check output that supports it.

Consider BAML when you need typed AI functions within an existing application. Its quickstart and language bridges offer a starting point for adding one component at a time. Before choosing a bridge, check the supported host language, runtime version and data types.

You could connect BAML application code to Kujo workflow tools through a process or service interface. We did not test a direct Kujo bridge, and support for another host language does not imply Kujo support. Define a versioned request/response format and test how failures cross the interface.

BAML’s type declarations, generated Python signatures, Pydantic models and model-response parser validate different parts of a call. In 0.22.2, an int identity function returned an invalid Python string unchanged, while an int-addition function given that string crashed an isolated Python process. Optional values and class decoding rejected other invalid fixtures. Use static checking and explicit validation for untrusted host inputs; the dedicated Python boundary review records which paths we tested. These results do not establish behavior in other releases, bridges or operating systems.

BAML 0.22.2 passed local function and assertion tests and rejected invalid source. Its generated Python client returned 42 synchronously and asynchronously; a standalone packed executable also returned 42. A local mock provider returned a typed object, while an invalid field and HTTP 401 produced distinct errors. Local trace queries recovered successful and failed runs with matching profiler counts. These fixtures do not test hosted models, cloud trace delivery, model quality or performance.

Stable language toolchain and Python bridge 0.22.2 (toolchain released 2026-10-13; commit 01f5c412c73c213846ea8cb6ead89d303b053672). Runtime and generated Python client tested on macOS x86_64. The nightly channel was not tested.
An agent-oriented language with AI functions and incremental host-language adoption.
Project diagnostics are implemented by the current check command.
Local assertions passed and failed as expected. Mock-provider response parsing accepted a valid object and rejected an invalid field; the full upstream suite was not run.
The 0.22.2 Python client passed sync/async calls, a packed executable returned 42, and loopback-provider response fixtures passed. Hosted models and other packaging targets were not tested.
A general dependent-type proof guarantee was not verified in the reviewed sources.

Local BTEL recordings and SQL queries recovered success/error outcomes and profiler counts. Trace context reached a generated-client call without leaking into the next call. Cloud delivery and overhead remain untested.
Is BAML just an LLM wrapper?
That description does not match the current project. The reviewed repository contains language checking and execution tooling; verify which generation of BAML a tutorial targets.
Does typed output prove an AI answer is right?
No. Type checks and structured parsing constrain representation. Domain correctness needs assertions, reference data or another suitable validation method.
Does the generated Python signature validate every runtime value?

No. In our 0.22.2 fixtures, static checking caught a wrong argument, but a direct Python identity call returned the wrong primitive type unchanged. Pydantic class decoding, optional values and model-response parsing had separate validation behavior. An invalid arithmetic input crashed the process. Validate untrusted host inputs explicitly and test the exact bridge version.
Compare BAML’s AI application tools with Kujo’s workflow checks and records.
Are you adopting an AI component, or governing an entire agent change?
Check the generation you are adopting

The pinned BAML source includes compiler diagnostics and a check command. Its current positioning includes an agent language and standalone runtime, so older prompt-DSL examples are not sufficient evidence for the current toolchain.
Pin the source or release before choosing syntax, examples and integration assumptions.
A valid data type can still contain the wrong answer

The inspected test command loads and runs compiled test sets. Our 0.22.2 fixture passed one assertion and failed a deliberately wrong expectation. This exercises a local test set, not the repository’s full suite. A typed or parsed AI response still needs checks for factual and domain correctness.
Pair type/shape checks with an independent domain-specific check and known wrong answers.

The Python bridge passed synchronous and asynchronous calls and propagated a declared error. Local tracing recorded outcomes and kept invocation context separate. Our deeper type-boundary tests distinguish static signatures, call argument checks, Pydantic class validation and model-response parsing. They also found a process crash for an invalid string passed to integer arithmetic in 0.22.2; valid arithmetic returned 42.
Test the exact host language, supported boundary types, failure propagation and retained trace data.

Commands, versions, failures and evidence tied to the actual revision.
Choose one AI function and the exact host language/runtime versions. Check the current quickstart against the pinned source; do not mix generations of examples.
Prepare malformed data, well-shaped but incorrect data, and a valid answer. Use the first to challenge representation checks and the second to challenge domain assertions.
Test exceptions, timeouts and boundary types in your own application. A documented bridge is not evidence that every required type or failure mode works for your chosen combination.
Store check/test output and the domain-specific check result with the code revision. Measure latency or token cost only with a declared model, configuration and repeated-run method.

These are separate checks, not one blanket type-safety guarantee. We tested the 0.22.2 CLI and Python bridge on macOS x86_64 with Python 3.10 and Pydantic 2.14.1. Each risky call ran in its own process. Official bridge docs describe type mappings and execution; the pinned source and fixtures establish the narrower behavior below.
Call echo(value: int) with a string in BAML source and typed Python.
BAML check rejected the call; mypy 2.4.0 rejected the generated Python call. Valid integer controls passed.
Static checks help when callers are checked. They do not automatically validate arbitrary values received at runtime.
Omit an argument, duplicate it, add an unknown name, pass an unsupported object or an oversized integer.
Argument names, serialization and numeric range checks are not a complete check of the declared parameter type.
Pass a string to int identity functions, or a mixed list to int[].
Sync and async identity calls returned the string. The mixed list also returned unchanged. An int? fixture rejected the string.
Validation varies by type and operation. The declared primitive return type did not enforce the observed result; do not generalize this to optional or class paths.
Construct Answer(value="bad"), or return a class with an invalid field.
Pydantic raised ValidationError. Answer(value="42") became Answer(value=42); strict validation rejected that string.
Class construction and decoding validate fields. A deliberately bypassed or later-mutated model could still yield a bad primitive field value.
Parse objects containing value 42, "bad", "42" and 41 through the generated function specification.
42 passed; "bad" raised ParseError; "42" was coerced to 42; 41 also passed.
Schema-aligned parsing can repair or coerce data. A structurally valid value is not proof that the answer meets a business requirement. These parser tests made no model request.
Call plus(value: int) -> int { value + 1 } with 41 and then "bad".
41 returned 42. The string caused SIGSEGV in separate processes, both with and without the sandbox.
This is a confirmed release/platform-specific failure, not a caught validation exception. Its native root cause and behavior on other targets remain unverified.
Validate the input with TypeAdapter(int).validate_python(value, strict=True) before calling BAML.
The numeric string was rejected; validated integer arithmetic returned 42.
This is an application-side guard tested for int. Validate the full input schema and retain domain-specific assertions; do not assume this one wrapper covers every BAML type.
Kujo vs Zerolang: workflow evidence and checked graph edits
Compare Kujo with Vercel Zerolang: task evidence, graph patches, type checks, executable tests and source projections, with pinned runtime results.

Vercel Zerolang makes the program graph the normal compiler input and lets agents submit checked semantic edits. Kujo combines language execution with separate tools for task requirements, output checks and run records. We inspected Zerolang’s repository and exercised release 0.3.4, including rejected patches and failing tests. These approaches address different parts of trusting agent-written software.

This page covers Vercel’s experimental Zerolang at zerolang.ai and vercel-labs/zerolang. The earlier page covered the unrelated systems-language preview at zero-lang.com. Its C++ and value-semantics descriptions do not describe this repository. We now pin this comparison to published Zerolang 0.3.4, rather than mixing its release behavior with current main.

Zerolang stores declarations, types, calls and related facts in zero.graph. Agents query and patch that graph; humans can export readable .0 projections. The normal package compile path consumes the graph. Our stale-hash and wrong-return-type patches failed without changing the stored graph. Kujo’s separate workflow tools check task contracts and observed outcomes; they do not provide this graph-editing model.

Evaluate Kujo when your main need is to define acceptance criteria, check generated artifacts or process outcomes, and retain evidence across a workflow. Plan the separate tools and their configuration. A successful kujo check in 1.8.2 is not a complete type-correctness guarantee.

Evaluate Zerolang when compiler-aware agent edits, graph queries and reviewable source projections fit your development process. Its checked patch interface gives agents a narrower editing surface than unrestricted text replacement. Treat it as an experiment: validate the graph shapes, platform and dependencies your application needs before adopting it.

A process or file boundary could connect a Zerolang component to external acceptance checks and run records. No direct Kujo integration was tested. Keep the graph hash, compiler version, test output and projection state together so a reviewer can connect a checked edit to the artifact that ran.

A valid graph can still implement the wrong behavior. Our graph check passed while a deliberately incorrect expected result made zero test fail. We did not establish general theorem proving, production sandbox security, cross-target support or a speed advantage. Runtime capability facts are not a substitute for an operating-system isolation boundary.

On macOS x86_64, release 0.3.4 initialized a package, applied a valid graph patch and ran a greeting. An addition test passed; changing its expectation failed. Stale and ill-typed patches left the graph unchanged. Projection export and verification passed, and edited projection text failed verification. These are small contract checks, not a workload benchmark or exhaustive compiler audit.
Canonical repository linked by zerolang.ai and its installer; distinct from zero-lang.com.
Graph-native programming for agent queries and checked semantic edits.
Stale-hash and wrong-return-type patches were rejected without changing the graph in our 0.3.4 fixtures.
The graph-backed package ran a greeting and an arithmetic test on macOS x64. Other targets were not executed.
General theorem proving was not established. Graph validation and executable tests answer narrower questions.
Graph hashes, structured patch outcomes and projection checks provide review evidence. A separate end-to-end run ledger was not assessed.
Vercel explicitly designs Zerolang for agents: they query a compiler-owned graph and submit checked edits. This design goal does not establish better productivity or correctness on every task.
Is this the Zero language at zero-lang.com?
No. This page now covers zerolang.ai and vercel-labs/zerolang. They are different projects, and the old systems-preview claims should not be carried across.
Does a checked graph prove the program meets its requirements?
No. Our valid graph passed check while a deliberately wrong test expectation failed. Keep type and structural validation separate from behavioral tests and external acceptance criteria.
Compare compiler-checked graph edits with task checks and retained workflow evidence.
Do you need a safer editing interface, evidence of the outcome, or both?

The graph stores program facts rather than treating source text as the only authority. Queries expose semantic handles; patch operations change those facts. The normal package compile path loads zero.graph.
Evaluate the actual edit and query operations your agent needs; do not infer lower token cost from the architecture alone.
Reject stale or invalid edits before saving

The inspected patch implementation checks the expected graph hash and validates graph shape. Executed release fixtures also rejected a Bool return in an i32 function. Both negative cases preserved the stored graph byte for byte.
This verifies two rejection paths, not every patch operation or concurrent-writer scenario.
Keep projections and graph state consistent

Export produces readable .0 text. Verify-projection detects divergence. Pinned documentation also describes automatic refresh when only source text changed, conflict errors when both sides changed, and ZERO_STALE=fail for stricter behavior.
Our export and drift fixtures passed. Automatic refresh, conflict resolution and merge behavior were inspected in documentation but not exercised.
Use external checks to enforce the task’s expected outcome.
Query graph facts and submit a patch with stale-state protection.
Before/after graph identity, patch result and independent acceptance output.
Retain the artifact and check output in a run record.
Export .0 text and verify projection consistency.
Readable diff plus a passing projection check; resolve conflicts explicitly.
Check the chosen deployment environment and isolation configuration.
Test the required backend, graph shape and target locally.
Target-specific build and execution evidence; our review covered macOS x64 only.
Use Zerolang 0.3.4 and record the downloaded binary hash. Check newer releases independently; do not assume main and a published binary behave identically.
Try a stale graph hash and a wrong return type. Require nonzero exits and verify that zero.graph did not change.
Run one passing assertion, then deliberately change its expected value. Record the failure and test count; a no-tests success is not behavioral coverage.
Export and verify the projection, then introduce drift and observe the diagnostic. Add your own task-level acceptance checks before considering deployment.
AI-native programming languages: a practical comparison
A decision guide to AI-native language claims, including Kujo, Bend and BAML, without conflating language safety with workflow evidence.

AI-native describes a design goal, not a safety certification. Compare what each language helps an agent do, which mistakes its tools can reject and what evidence you can inspect after a run. The right choice depends on your application and the guarantees it needs.
Three different questions behind the label

Ask three questions separately: does the language help you build AI-powered applications, help an agent write and inspect code, or help a reviewer check the result? A project may address one well without addressing the others. Choose which of these matters for your application before starting a trial.

Kujo combines language execution with separate tools for task requirements, output checks and run records. Bend emphasizes laws, proofs and parallel computation. BAML emphasizes AI functions and application integration. Vercel Zerolang gives agents a graph-query and checked-patch interface. The direct comparisons identify the pinned versions, executed checks and remaining limits.
Keep established languages in the evaluation

Keep Python, TypeScript and Rust in the evaluation when their libraries, deployment options and your team’s experience already suit the application. A new language needs to justify the cost of adopting it with a capability you need. Tests and execution records can also support agent-written code in an established language.
How to choose the best fit

Use one representative repository task and fix its acceptance criteria before the agent starts. Record versions, dependencies, checks, outputs and manual repairs. Include an incorrect output that the checker must reject. Compare maintenance and integration work alongside correctness; a small syntax example cannot establish overall productivity.
What this guide does not rank

We do not rank market share, search volume, speed or agent success rates. These pages distinguish inspected implementation from official claims and unknowns. A useful performance comparison would need the same workloads, appropriate targets and repeated measurements.
What is the best AI-native programming language?

There is no supported universal ranking here. Use Bend’s proof model, BAML’s current application and bridge model, or Kujo’s workflow tools when they fit a concrete requirement, then test that requirement on the pinned toolchain.
Choose a language by what it can do.
Compare each language’s design and the evidence behind its guarantees.
What does “AI-native” need to mean for your project?
Diagnostics, clear interfaces and a workable edit–check loop.
Independent evidence against your actual requirements.

Typed AI functions, model calls and host-language integration belong to the application design question. BAML’s current positioning is relevant here, but a bridge still needs validation for the host, types and version you plan to ship.
Trial one real feature inside the existing application before proposing a rewrite.
Decide exactly what you need to check

Bend’s laws and proofs address formally stated properties. Kujo’s compiler checks, non-fatal interpreter type diagnostics and separate outcome tools answer different questions. Decide whether the requirement is a universal invariant, an observed behavior, or a reviewable delivery process.
Ask for the exact proposition or assertion, then inspect the assumptions around it.
Compare against the language you already use

A new language changes more than syntax: build integration, dependencies, debugging and maintenance all matter. Keep Python, TypeScript or Rust in the evaluation when one already supports the application; the AI-native label alone is not a migration case.
Record integration work and manual repairs alongside successful outputs.
Compare the options for your application.
These are entry points for a trial, not rankings. Sources establish the reviewed scope; the trial criteria are editorial recommendations.
Language execution plus separate task, evaluation and evidence tools.
Selecting and configuring an ecosystem is part of the adoption cost.
One repository change with explicit criteria and retained check output.
Laws, proof definitions and documented parallel targets.
A checked law still needs the right specification and a reviewed trust boundary.
One precise invariant plus a deliberately broken proof or law.
Agent-oriented application code, AI functions and host integration.
Generated signatures, dynamic host inputs and parsed model outputs have different validation paths. Test each separately; a valid value can still be wrong.
One typed AI function with malformed and well-typed wrong responses.
Graph queries, checked semantic patches and readable source projections.
Experimental; our runtime review covers small macOS x64 fixtures, not production or cross-target readiness.
Reject a stale patch, reject a type mismatch, and make a behavioral test fail.
Your application’s libraries, tests and deployment environment.
An ecosystem name does not guarantee the specific integration you need.
Use the same task and acceptance criteria as the new-language candidates.
The fit of its programming model and deployment constraints.
Include implementation effort, required libraries and team familiarity in the decision.
Compare a representative component in the existing application using the same output checks.
Choose a real change with a bounded input, expected output and failure cases. Keep the acceptance criteria identical across candidates; do not reward one candidate with an easier workload.
Record runtime, source revision, libraries, deployment target and any model configuration. Document unavailable dependencies instead of substituting a different task silently.
Include failed attempts, manual edits, integration time and failing controls. A small successful syntax demo does not estimate repository-level maintenance effort.
Separate correctness, integration fit and operational cost. A candidate that does not meet a required boundary should not win because an unrelated benchmark looks good.
Ask for evidence behind each claim.

A representative task set, all attempts and independent acceptance checks.
Whether the result transfers to your repository, model and maintenance cycle.
A malformed response rejected and a valid response accepted.
Whether a valid response is factually or operationally correct.

Whether the law captures the requirement and external code respects the interface.
Commands, inputs, revisions, artifacts and linked raw check outcomes.

An AI-native label is not a certification
AI-native has no standardized assurance level in this guide. Ask which mechanism provides the claimed confidence.
A small demo does not measure productivity
A tiny program can omit packaging, migration, debugging and recovery costs. Evaluate a representative task.
An unknown capability is not necessarily unsupported
Missing verification is an evidence gap. Preserve it as unknown rather than awarding a negative capability score.
Programming languages for AI agents: choosing the host and tools
Choose a language for building and supervising agents by tool contracts, failure handling, deployment and the evidence your workflow needs.

Choose an agent’s host language by the tools it must call, the permissions those tools need and the failures it must recover from. The host coordinates the agent; the repository it edits can use another language. Test the interfaces between them before deciding whether any language change is needed.
Choose the agent host separately from the code it edits

The agent host coordinates model calls and tools. The repository it edits may use a different language, so choosing a host does not require rewriting the application. Record both runtimes and test how generated changes move through the build and execution process.

List the provider interfaces, application libraries, operating systems and deployment environments you need. Include Python or TypeScript when they already host your application, and Rust when its programming model suits the work. Check specific library versions; a language name does not guarantee an integration.

Kujo’s Agents SDK provides workflow primitives as a library. Dispatch adds workflow coordination and reviewable run state. Workcell addresses configured execution boundaries, while Watchdog records telemetry. These are separate projects, not language syntax. Choose the components you need and check what each controls. Agents SDK 1.1.3 uses cooperative budget and cancellation checks; callbacks must enforce their own deadlines. The host supplies provider credentials, permissions and persistence. Check each tool’s own runtime pin: Workcell 1.2.0 documents Kujo 1.6.0, so the site’s Kujo 1.8.2 baseline is not a tested compatibility claim for every tool.

BAML describes typed AI functions and bridges into existing applications. Bend’s laws and proofs may suit a component with precisely stated invariants. Either option still requires controls on external tools, validation of their outputs and a plan for failed or interrupted operations. BAML’s Python boundary review distinguishes static checks from dynamic input validation and model-response parsing.

Test that denied actions remain denied, interrupted tasks have explicit outcomes, malformed tool results are rejected and retries do not duplicate effects. Report fixture tests separately from live-provider tests. A deterministic fixture checks that path through the application; it does not establish provider reliability or production isolation.
Start with one workflow you can test

Build one tool-calling workflow with offline fixtures, then add one live provider with explicit credentials and limits. Keep the task input, versions, tool results and independent checks. The workflow guide shows how to turn those records into evidence a reviewer can inspect.
Must the agent host and target repository use the same language?
No. A host can invoke tools that inspect or build another language. Verify the process, data and permission boundaries instead of assuming shared syntax provides safety.
Choose how your agent runs and uses tools.
Choose the agent host, its tools and the repository it edits separately.
Which component owns each action, failure and recovery?
Coordinates model requests, tool selection and run state.
Validates requests and controls external effects.
Keeps its own language, build system and acceptance checks.
The host and application can use different languages

The host chooses how to coordinate model calls and tool results; the target repository can use another language. Kujo’s Agents SDK is a library layer with explicit adapter boundaries and offline fixtures, not a reason to translate every repository it touches.
Pin both runtimes and verify the data/process boundary between them.

Dispatch documents workflow orchestration and reviewable run state. Treat interrupted work and replay as application design concerns: know what completed, what remains uncertain and which external effects would be unsafe to repeat.
Test interruption around a side effect, not only between harmless model calls.

Workcell’s execution receipts and Watchdog’s telemetry address different aspects of a run. Recording an attempted operation does not itself prevent it; the configured execution boundary must enforce the intended restriction.
Observe both the reported denial and the absence of the prohibited effect.
Choose the host by the interfaces it must own.
Use these criteria to evaluate your actual stack. The failure probes are proposed tests, not claims that a language automatically enforces them.
Which provider, model and response shape must the host support?
Return malformed or incomplete data from an offline adapter fixture.
Pinned adapter version, input, validation outcome and error details.
Where are names, arguments and domain constraints checked?
Request an unknown tool and a known tool with an invalid argument.
Rejected request and confirmation that no tool effect occurred.
Which actions can run, need approval or must remain denied?
Attempt an operation outside the allowed scope.
Policy/configuration, denial result and independently observed side effects.
Which operations are safe to repeat and how are duplicates detected?
Interrupt after an external effect but before its acknowledgement.
Operation identity, recovery decision and final effect count.
How does the host build and inspect a repository in another language?
Return a nonzero build exit and a stale output artifact.
Actual revision, command, exit, stdout/stderr and artifact identity.
Which run/step/tool identifiers connect the records?
Drop or mismatch a correlation identifier in a fixture.
Raw event chain and an explicit incomplete-evidence result.
Draw the host, model adapter, tools and target repository as separate components. Mark each place where data or execution authority crosses a boundary.
Use deterministic model/tool fixtures and run success, denial, malformed-result and interruption cases. Label those results as fixtures, not live-provider evidence.
Use a single required provider and a narrowly scoped tool. Record configuration and limits, then test the error path as well as the successful response.
Introduce timeouts and interrupted effects deliberately. Require an explicit final state and inspect whether retrying produced duplicate work before broadening the deployment.
A retry can be correct code and the wrong action.

Bend’s guide describes laws and proof definitions. A checked proof addresses a stated property under the proof system’s assumptions, rather than a finite set of test inputs. Workcell receipts and RunLedger records help show what ran and what was reported. RunLedger accepts supplied test results and verdicts, so follow the links to the underlying evidence. Choose checks by failure mode. Validate structure and values for malformed output, test execution controls for unauthorized effects, and run behavioral tests for regressions. Investigate a suitable proof system for a universal mathematical invariant. Use explicit gates for release requirements, and state what each result establishes.

It establishes that the suite’s assertions passed under the recorded conditions. Completion also requires the suite to cover the acceptance criteria, to execute against the actual deliverable, and to preserve failures rather than hiding them.

Verify agent workflows: contracts, checks and reproducible evidence
A practical guide to verifying AI-generated code, evaluating coding agents and preserving traceable execution evidence with honest limits.

Check an agent’s completion report against the work it produced. Define the requirement first, inspect the output with an independent checker and keep the commands, results and environment details needed to repeat the check. This guide shows how to connect those steps using a small runnable example.
1. Write the acceptance contract before implementation

Describe observable behavior, allowed changes and failure cases before implementation. Spec can validate the structure of a task record, but you must decide whether its requirements are sufficient. For example, require a generated JSON object to contain an integer total of 42, rather than merely requiring a file to exist.

Use a checker that does not simply repeat the agent’s implementation. Read the generated output, parse it and check its fields and values. Eval provides configurable checks; the example below uses a separate Python checker to show the principle. Keep that checker outside the agent’s write access when your threat model requires it.
3. Test the verifier with a known failure

Run the checker against a correct output, then an intentionally wrong one. Require the wrong output to produce a nonzero verifier exit. If both pass, the checker cannot detect that error. This control shows that one selected failure is detectable, not that every error or malicious change will be caught.

Record the repository commit, runtime version, commands, exit codes and output hashes. Keep useful stdout and stderr while controlling secrets and retention. RunLedger stores metadata and supplied results; Workcell records configured execution. Distinguish caller-supplied pass labels from independently observed results.

Fixed commands and inputs make a check easier to repeat. Live APIs, model sampling, time and changing dependencies can still affect the result. Use offline fixtures for deterministic checks and report live runs separately. A replayed fixture is not a fresh provider response.

Review the actual diff and map each acceptance criterion to its evidence. ShipCheck can add release checks, while a human or authorized gate makes the decision. Treat missing evidence as unresolved rather than assuming success.

Download [produce.kujo](/compare/evidence/produce.kujo) and [verify.py](/compare/evidence/verify.py) into the same directory. Run `KUJO_BIN=/path/to/kujo python3 verify.py` with Kujo 1.8.2. The test runner checks correct and incorrect outputs, then writes evidence.json with command results, environment details and hashes. It uses no network or model credentials. See the [methodology](/compare/evidence/README.md).

A pass shows that the checker accepted the correct output and rejected the specified invalid cases for this small task. It does not compare languages, evaluate a coding agent or prove an application correct. To evaluate an agent, use representative tasks, record all attempts and configurations, and report manual intervention. Do not turn this exercise into a general success-rate claim.
How do I prove an agent completed a task?

Map every acceptance criterion to an independently checked deliverable, preserve the results and review any remaining conditions. A final chat message or recorded pass label alone is not that evidence.
